From the surgery

Loneliness needs care too

Unwanted loneliness affects physical and mental health. Primary care is a good place to detect it and to connect people with their community.

By Alejandro Rosàs, family doctor

Many older people come to the surgery regularly, and not always for an urgent medical reason. Sometimes the visit is also one of the few moments in the week when someone asks how they are. Unwanted loneliness is common, and not only among older people: young people, carers and newcomers to a city also experience it.

Psychology distinguishes between social isolation (having few contacts, something that can be counted) and loneliness (the feeling that the relationships we have are not enough). One can be surrounded by people and feel lonely, and live alone without feeling lonely.

Why it matters for health

Studies have associated loneliness and isolation with worse cardiovascular health, more depression, poorer sleep and higher mortality, with effects comparable to other known risk factors. It is not a minor or merely "social" matter.

What can be done from the surgery

The first step is to ask, naturally: "Who do you talk to during the week?". The second is to know the local resources: associations, community centres, group activities, volunteering programmes. So-called social prescribing consists precisely in connecting the person with those community activities, and it is spreading in many health centres.

Psychology contributes a useful idea: relationships are built through repeated, meaningful contact. "Going out more" is not enough; it helps to find activities with a shared purpose and some regularity, where encounters repeat and trust has time to grow.
